"The power of this bust will not just be in the metal that delineates Sojourner Truth's face; it will also be in the message that defines her legacy. **WASHINGTON** — Lawmakers, historians, civil rights advocates and cultural figures gathered in the U.S. Capitol's Emancipation Hall on Thursday for the "Celebration of Truth," a ceremony honoring the enduring legacy of abolitionist and women's rights pioneer Sojourner Truth.

The event, held beneath the soaring dome of the Capitol Visitor Center, blended solemn tribute with soaring artistic expression, drawing an audience that filled the hall to capacity. Organizers described the gathering as both a commemoration of history and a call to continued action.

## A Voice That Still Echoes

The ceremony's emotional centerpiece came with a dramatic recitation of Truth's famous 1851 speech, "Ain't I A Woman," delivered at the Women's Convention in Akron, Ohio. The performance drew a standing ovation from attendees, many of whom were visibly moved.

"When Sojourner Truth asked that question more than 170 years ago, she was demanding that this nation see the full humanity of Black women," one speaker told the crowd. "That question still challenges us today."

The words — questioning the contradictions of a society that claimed to protect women while denying that protection to those who were enslaved — resonated throughout the marble hall, punctuated by applause and murmurs of affirmation.

## Speeches Reflect on History and Progress

A series of speakers took the podium to reflect on Truth's contributions and the broader struggle for equality that she came to symbolize.

Speakers emphasized the intersection of the abolitionist and women's suffrage movements, noting that Truth stood at the crossroads of both causes at a time when few dared to speak so boldly.

"She could not read or write, yet her words have outlived those of presidents and generals," one dignitary noted. "That is the power of truth spoken plainly and courageously."

Several speakers connected the historical struggle to contemporary conversations about voting rights, representation and social justice, urging attendees to view the commemoration not as a closing chapter but as an ongoing responsibility.

## Music Fills the Hall

Between remarks, musical performances lent the ceremony a spirit of celebration. A choir performed selections rooted in the tradition of spirituals — the same songs of hope and endurance that once sustained enslaved communities.

The rich harmonies filled Emancipation Hall, at times drawing the audience to its feet. A soloist's rendition of a gospel classic brought a hush over the room before erupting into applause.

The musical program was designed, organizers said, to reflect the arc of the African American experience — from suffering and struggle toward triumph and hope.

## A Fitting Setting

The choice of Emancipation Hall as the venue carried its own symbolic weight. The space, part of the Capitol Visitor Center, honors the enslaved laborers who helped construct the Capitol building itself.

For many attendees, holding a tribute to Sojourner Truth in that particular hall represented a powerful convergence of memory and meaning.

"There could be no more fitting place," one organizer said. "We stand in a hall built in part by enslaved hands, honoring a woman who devoted her life to freedom."

## Looking Forward

As the ceremony drew to a close, speakers encouraged those in attendance to carry Truth's message beyond the walls of the Capitol.

The "Celebration of Truth" concluded with a final musical number and a moment of reflection, leaving many in the audience contemplating the distance traveled since Truth first posed her defiant question — and the road that still lies ahead.
